items.followUp: State one similarity and one difference between Dobereiner’s triads and Newlands’ law of octaves.

rubric.why: A triad is a group of three elements with similar properties.
rubric.description: Identifies the group as three elements with similar properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that there are three elements and that they have similar properties.

rubric.why: The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.
rubric.description: States the atomic-mass relationship within a triad.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the approximate mean relationship.

modelAnswer: Dobereiner arranged some elements in groups of three, called triads, whose elements had similar chemical properties.
In each triad, the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.

items.followUp: Explain how inner-shell electrons affect the attraction between the nucleus and valence electrons.

rubric.why: Inner-shell electrons shield outer electrons from the nucleus.
rubric.description: Identifies the shielding role of inner-shell electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that inner electrons shield or reduce the nuclear attraction on outer electrons.

rubric.why: The effective attraction of the nucleus on valence electrons is reduced.
rubric.description: States the effect on the attraction experienced by valence electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the effective nuclear attraction on valence electrons is less or reduced.

modelAnswer: The shielding effect is the reduction in the attraction between the nucleus and valence electrons due to the presence of inner-shell electrons.
The inner electrons shield the outer electrons from the positive charge of the nucleus.

items.followUp: Write two properties of covalent compounds.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points because of strong electrostatic forces between their ions.
rubric.description: Gives the high melting and boiling points of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating their high melting and boiling points.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.
rubric.description: Gives an electrical-conductivity property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating conductivity in a molten or aqueous state, or lack of conductivity in the solid state.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: Define ductility and name one metal that shows it.

rubric.why: Malleability is the property that allows a substance, especially a metal, to be hammered or beaten into sheets.
rubric.description: Defines malleability as the ability to be beaten or hammered into sheets.
rubric.how: Award both marks for a clear definition; award 1 mark for identifying the ability to be shaped and 1 for specifying sheets.

modelAnswer: Malleability is the ability of a metal to be hammered or beaten into thin sheets.

rubric.why: Any one correct example of a suspension earns credit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example, such as muddy water or chalk in water.

rubric.why: A second distinct correct example completes the requested pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid example distinct from the first.

modelAnswer: Chalk powder in water is another suspension.

items.followUp: Define a saturated solution and give one example.

rubric.why: In an aqueous solution, water is the solvent.
rubric.description: Defines an aqueous solution by identifying water as its solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a solution in which water acts as the solvent.

rubric.why: A solution of a substance such as salt or sugar in water is an example.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one suitable example.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
For example, salt dissolved in water is an aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Calculate the mass/volume percentage of a solution containing 5 g of solute in 100 mL of solution.

rubric.why: Volume/volume percentage is calculated as the volume of solute divided by the volume of solution, multiplied by 100.
rubric.description: States the formula for volume/volume percentage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio and multiplication by 100.

rubric.why: A mixture made up to 100 mL of solution using 10 mL of ethanol has a volume/volume concentration of 10%.
rubric.description: Provides a correctly identified volume/volume example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example with matching volumes and percentage.

modelAnswer: Volume/volume percentage is the volume of solute present in 100 volumes of solution.
Volume/volume percentage = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100.
For example, if 10 mL of ethanol is present in 100 mL of solution, the concentration is 10% v/v.

items.followUp: Define malleability and ductility, giving one example of a metal for each property.

rubric.why: Malleable metals can be hammered or beaten into sheets.
rubric.description: Explains what is meant by malleable metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking malleability with forming sheets by beating or hammering.

rubric.why: Ductile metals can be drawn into wires.
rubric.description: Explains what is meant by ductile metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking ductility with being drawn into wires.

modelAnswer: Malleable metals can be hammered or beaten into thin sheets.
Ductile metals can be drawn into wires.
